notes.meaning: Israel packed up their tents at Mithkah and traveled to Hashmonah. This stop was one of many during their long wandering in the wilderness, where God continued to guide and feed them. Although the exact location is unknown today, God had Moses record each stage to show His faithful care along every step of the journey.

The people set out from Hashmonah and made their camp at Moseroth. Moseroth is another form of the name Mosera, which was near Mount Hor where Aaron was later buried. God kept the nation moving under the guidance of the pillar of cloud, taking them through the desert according to His timing.

Leaving Moseroth, the camp moved on to Bene-jaakan, a name meaning the wells of the sons of Jaakan. This place was named after a local Horite clan who had originally dug water wells there. God led His people to places where their flocks could find water even in the dry desert.

The Israelites departed from Bene-jaakan and set up camp at Hor-haggidgad. The name means a cavern or hollow, and it appears elsewhere in Scripture as Gudgodah. God safely guided the vast congregation through rough ravines and rocky country without losing their way.

From Hor-haggidgad, the people traveled to Jotbathah. Scripture describes this place as a land of flowing streams and brooks. After passing through parched land, God brought His people to a refreshing oasis where there was plenty of water.

Israel pulled up their tent pegs at Jotbathah and camped at Abronah. The name means a crossing place or passage. Very little else is known about this stop, but it marked another stage along their southern route toward the sea.

The camp journeyed from Abronah down to Ezion-geber on the shore of the Red Sea. This was a well-known harbor at the tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, where King Solomon would later station his ships. Reaching this port brought the Israelites to the southernmost point of their wanderings.

Israel turned north from Ezion-geber and returned to Kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin. This arrival marked the end of the thirty-eight long years of wandering that followed the nation's rebellion. The new generation was now assembled back at the threshold of the Promised Land.

The people set out from Kadesh and pitched their camp at Mount Hor on the border of Edom. Because the king of Edom refused to let them travel through his land, Israel had to stay along the outer edge. This mountain was the chosen place where Aaron's earthly journey would come to an end.

Aaron the high priest went up Mount Hor at the Lord's direct command and died there. This took place on the first day of the fifth month, in the fortieth year after Israel left Egypt. Even though his death was a punishment for his lack of faith at Meribah, Aaron finished his life in humble obedience to God.

Aaron was 123 years old when he died on the top of Mount Hor. God had blessed him with unusual strength and a long life so he could shepherd Israel's worship through nearly all forty wilderness years. His long life was a testimony to the Lord's patience and mercy.

While Israel was camped near Mount Hor, the Canaanite king of Arad in the southern desert heard they were coming. This note looks back to Israel's first real battle against a Canaanite king, which the Lord helped them win. It served as a reminder that their wandering was closing and the battle for Canaan was starting.

Israel departed from Mount Hor to go around Edom and set up their camp at Zalmonah. The name of this place is connected to the word for an image, and early writers linked it with the bronze serpent Moses lifted up in the desert. God protected the people even as the road became difficult and tiring.

The Israelites broke camp at Zalmonah and traveled on to Punon. This station was situated in the rough hill country east of Edom. God continued to sustain the entire nation as they steadily marched north.

From Punon, the people moved on and camped at Oboth. The name Oboth means water bags, which may suggest a dry area where travelers had to carry their own water supply. Through every dry stretch, God faithfully provided what His people needed to survive.

Leaving Oboth, Israel camped at Iye-abarim, right along the southern border of Moab. The name refers to the heaps or ruins of the border country. Reaching this spot meant the Israelites had successfully bypassed Edom and were approaching the Jordan valley.

The people set out from Iyim and encamped at Dibon-gad. This town was later rebuilt and occupied by the tribe of Gad, which is how it received its full name. Each new camp brought the tribes closer to receiving their promised territory.

The camp moved forward from Dibon-gad and stopped at Almon-diblathaim. This town sat in land that once belonged to Moab before the Amorites conquered it. God was leading Israel straight through territory that used to belong to powerful kingdoms.

Israel journeyed up to the mountains of Abarim and camped facing Mount Nebo. Mount Nebo is the famous peak where Moses would soon view the Promised Land before his death. The people were now resting on the very heights that overlooked their future home.

The Israelites came down from the mountains and camped on the plains of Moab beside the Jordan River, right across from Jericho. This was their final major encampment of the forty-year journey. Here the nation remained while Moses reviewed God's laws and prepared them to enter the land.

The camp of Israel was huge, stretching along the Jordan from Beth-jeshimoth all the way to Abel-shittim. Abel-shittim means the meadow of acacia trees, and it also recalled the deep mourning after the people sinned at Peor. After decades of wandering in barren sand, God brought the whole nation safely to the river's edge.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Church Fathers saw the forty-two encampments as symbols of the stages of a Christian's journey, leaving sin behind to grow in virtue toward heaven.

notes.meaning: While Israel was camped by the Jordan across from Jericho, the Lord gave fresh commands to Moses. This begins an important new section laying out the rules for conquering and settling Canaan. God was preparing His people for the responsibilities waiting for them on the other side of the river.

Moses was instructed to tell the Israelites how to act the moment they crossed the Jordan into Canaan. Taking the land was not just about finding homes, but about obeying God's special mission. Their new life in the land required complete faithfulness to the Lord from the start.

God commanded Israel to drive out all the Canaanites and completely destroy their carved stones, metal idols, and hilltop shrines. No monuments of false worship were to be kept as souvenirs or house decorations. God demanded this complete removal so His people would never be lured into the evil practices of the heathen nations.

The people were told to take possession of the land and settle down in it because God Himself was giving it to them. Emptying the land of idolatry and settling in it belonged together as part of God's single promise. The land was not won by their own power, but received as a gift from the Lord.

The land was to be divided among the clans by casting lots, giving larger areas to bigger tribes and smaller areas to smaller tribes. Using the lot showed that God alone decided where each family would live, preventing jealousy and arguments among the tribes. In this way, every clan received its proper inheritance under God's watchful care.

God warned that if Israel failed to drive out the Canaanites, the survivors would become like blinding barbs in their eyes and sharp thorns in their sides. They would constantly harass the Israelites, lead them into sin, and bring them misery. Indulging what God calls evil always produces deep pain and spiritual danger in the end.

The Lord gave a solemn final warning that if Israel copied the ways of the Canaanites, He would judge them and drive them out of the land instead. God does not overlook sin in His own people. Staying securely in the Promised Land required wholehearted obedience to the Lord.
